title: GPU pool scaling breadcrumbs (personal scratchpad)
content:
Quick notes / breadcrumbs from the dedicated GPU pool thrash incident (scratchpad). Personal log — messy. Use these to recreate timeline and commands I ran.

TL;DR:
- Symptom: sudden latency spike + 503s for hosted requests around 2025-01-23 03:20-03:50 UTC.
- Observed: autoscaler spun up nodes rapidly then immediately scaled down (thrash). Warmup/model-load times ~90–220s per pod causing queue buildup.
- Hypothesis: scale-down cooldown too short and scale-up provisioning slow for chosen instance family. Also a bunch of short-lived bursts (small traffic spikes) causing reactive scaling.

Timeline + quick clues (local timestamps):
- 2025-01-23 03:18 UTC: first error spike reported by Sentry, tokenized alerts from paging.
- 03:20: k8s HPA saw CPU/queue > target on deployment/redwood-serving (batchers).
- 03:21: cluster-autoscaler (CA) started provisioning 4 nodes (p4d-ish).
- 03:22–03:26: pods scheduled but remained in Init/Warmup due to model pull + loader step; pod status "ContainerCreating" -> "Running" but loader container logs showed model load time 90–120s.
- 03:28: CA scaled down one node because utilization metric dipped; pods got evicted and restarted -> repeated model load.
- 03:42: system recovered after manual intervention (increased scale-down-delay and pinned some baseline capacity).

Commands I ran (copy/paste-able):
- kubectl get pods -n redwood-serving -o wide --show-labels
- kubectl describe hpa redwood-serving -n redwood-serving
- kubectl logs deployment/redwood-serving -c model-loader -n redwood-serving --since=2h | grep -E "loading|model|failed|OOM|error" -n
- kubectl get nodes -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,TYPE:.metadata.labels.beta\\.kubernetes\\.io/instance-type,CPU:.status.capacity.cpu,GPU:.status.allocatable.nvidia\\.com/gpu
- kubectl get events -n kube-system --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -n 50
- aws autoscaling describe-scaling-activities --auto-scaling-group-name redwood-gpu-asg --region us-west-2 --max-items 20
- aws ec2 describe-instances --filters "Name=tag:KubernetesCluster,Values=redwood-prod" --region us-west-2

Snippets I saw in logs: (copied verbatim, redacted IDs)
- "model-loader: INFO model download started for model 'llama-65b-8k' (s3://models/llama-65b-8k.tar.gz)"
- "model-loader: WARN failed to fetch shard-3, retrying (http 503)"
- "kernel-init: error: cudaMalloc failed: out of memory"
- "kubelet: eviction threshold reached: node pressure: memory"
- "cluster-autoscaler: ScaleDown: candidate nodes found (low utilization) -> scale down node/node-xyz"
- "kube-scheduler: 0/7 nodes are available: Insufficient gpu."

Observations / metrics notes:
- Model cold-load time: 90–220s depending on IO and shard retries. Large models (65B) dominated.
- Node provisioning (PAI from cloud): 2–5 minutes median time to Ready after CA request depending on AZ capacity.
- Scale-down heuristic: CA used CPU/utilization window of 1m with scaleDownUnneededTime=2m. That was too short for model warmup patterns.
- Batcher behavior: incoming short bursts of 10–30 qps — batcher attempts to scale pods but each pod costs long warmup; over-provisioning for transient spike is wasteful but under-provisioning causes latency SLO failures.

Hypotheses to validate:
1) scale-down cooldown too aggressive. Node/pod warmup >> scaleDownUnneededTime leading to thrash.
2) CA picks instance types with limited regional capacity; provisioning variance increases latency — fallback instance families aren't prioritized.
3) model-loader not checkpointing partial loads; evicted pods restart full load loop. Should support resume/KV cache warm restore.
4) HPA metric choice (CPU) is noisy for cold-start-heavy workloads; need a queue length or custom metric (pending requests or ready-models) to drive scaling.
5) kubelet eviction and OOMs indicate pod memory request/limits mismatched for quantized models leading to preemption.

Things I tried (and results):
- Bumped scaleDownUnneededTime to 10m in cluster-autoscaler config (local test) -> thrash reduced in canary but baseline cost increased.
- Created a small pool of always-on "warm" nodes (2 nodes) with taint + toleration so critical serving pods land there -> recovered SLOs immediately in staging.
- Adjusted HPA from CPU to a custom metric (http_queue_length) in a sidecar exporter and HPA based on that metric -> improved responsiveness in stress tests.
- Tried node labels + preferredSchedulingTerms to prefer instance families with local NVMe for model cache; saw ~20% faster cold-loads.
- Disabled aggressive CA scale-down on ASG (set min=2) -> stops thrash but increases cost.

Commands/patches used (examples):
- kubectl patch deployment redwood-serving -n redwood-serving -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"tolerations":[{"key":"warm-node","operator":"Exists","effect":"NoSchedule"}]}}}}'
- kubectl apply -f hpa-queue-length.yaml (HPA using custom metrics adapter)
- aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name redwood-gpu-asg --min-size 2 --region us-west-2

Open questions / things to drill into next:
- Can loader support incremental materialization or persistent cache (PV) for model shards so restarts aren't full reloads?
- Should we adopt a two-tier pool: very small always-ready pool + burstable cold pool? Trade-offs and pricing (preemptible/spot).
- Are there cloud quota limits or instance limits causing provision delays for certain instance families in us-west-2? Need to check capacity-optimization logs.
- How noisy is CPU as a signal across different request patterns? Get histograms and test with bursty synthetic workload.
- Evaluate using Karpenter instead of CA for faster provisioning and heterogeneous families (if allowed).

Minimal repro steps (local simulation):
1) Start redwood-serving with model X pinned to big config but only 1 baseline replica.
2) Send synthetic burst pattern: 30 qps for 1m, then 0 for 3m, repeat (use vegeta or k6).
3) Track HPA, CA, node events, and model-loader logs.
4) Measure time from HPA decision -> pod ready -> model-ready (loader log).

Notes to self (less structured):
- Maya had an idea to use instance-store NVMe to cache shards across pods on same node. Worth prototyping (needs hostPath/PVC + eviction handling).
- Diego mentioned we should add a warmup_probe that marks a pod "serving-ready" only after KV cache warm. That would give HPA/Ingress better signal.
- For immediate mitigation in prod: set min-size of ASG to 2 and annotate critical pods to prefer warm nodes.

Potential quick patch (low-risk):
- HPA switch metric + set min replicas=2 for critical deployment + increase scaleDownUnneededTime for CA to 10m. Roll as config change behind feature flag.

Next actions I will take (ordered):
1) Open small RFC: two-tier pool + warm-node pattern (short doc). (owner: me)
2) Prototype PV-backed shard cache on staging with hostPath fallback. (owner: Maya)
3) Add warmup_ready probe and metric export for "model_ready". (owner: Diego)
4) Short-term: change ASG min-size and CA scale-down config for prod (ops runbook). (owner: oncall)

End of scratchpad. Will extract into a cleaner incident postmortem after validating logs and metrics.

-- Riley
